fuentes/la-civilizacion-de-la-diosa/titu.texto: The Civilization of the Goddess: The World of Old Europe

fuentes/la-civilizacion-de-la-diosa/resu.texto: Gimbutas's final synthesis of Neolithic Europe. It describes an “Old Europe” of unfortified farming villages, egalitarian between the sexes and centered on the worship of a goddess, with a writing system of its own (the Vinča signs), which, according to her, was destroyed by waves of patriarchal herders and warriors from the steppe, the “kurgans,” bearers of the Indo-European languages.

fuentes/la-civilizacion-de-la-diosa/por_.texto: It is the text that brought the kurgan hypothesis to the general public and inspired spiritual feminism. Archaeologists such as Lynn Meskell (1995) and Ruth Tringham objected that it reads the figurines as mother goddesses without evidence, that there are no signs of an egalitarian or woman-centered order, and that it projects a modern ideal onto the Neolithic. The 2015 genetic studies confirmed a large arrival of steppe ancestry around 3000–2500 BC, but say nothing about religion or gender roles, so her portrait of Old Europe still has no support.

fuentes/archaeology-and-language/titulo.texto: Archaeology and Language: The Puzzle of Indo-European Origins

fuentes/archaeology-and-language/resumen.texto: Renfrew proposes that the Indo-European languages spread across Europe with agriculture, from Anatolia around 7000 BC, through the slow advance of farmers rather than through conquest. In the chapter on the Celts he argues that Celtic did not arrive with Iron Age invasions but formed locally, in western Europe, from the languages of the first farmers.

fuentes/archaeology-and-language/por_que.texto: It dismantled the old idea of “Celtic invasions” as the automatic explanation for every cultural change. Mallory and Anthony objected that the shared vocabulary for wheel, wagon and wool forces Proto-Indo-European to be dated after 4000 BC, and the 2015 ancient DNA studies supported a migration from the steppe. Some phylogenetic studies of language (Gray and Atkinson, 2003) did favor his chronology, and Heggarty et al. (2023) propose a “hybrid” model, with a root about 8,100 years ago south of the Caucasus and a later branch through the steppe.

fuentes/in-search-of-the-indo-europeans/.texto: In Search of the Indo-Europeans: Language, Archaeology and Myth

It reviews what can be reconstructed of Proto-Indo-European (its vocabulary for animals, plants, techniques, kinship and gods) and compares hypotheses about its homeland. It concludes that the most coherent with linguistics and archaeology is the Pontic-Caspian steppe between 4500 and 2500 BC.

It has been the standard reference on the Indo-European problem for more than thirty years. Its critics (Renfrew and the defenders of an Anatolian origin) objected that archaeology shows no clear invasion from the steppe into western Europe, an objection that ancient DNA weakened in 2015.

fuentes/the-horse-the-wheel-and-language.texto: The Horse, the Wheel, and Language: How Bronze-Age Riders from the Eurasian Steppes Shaped the Modern World

Anthony dates Proto-Indo-European from its chariot vocabulary (between 4000 and 3500 BC) and places it in the steppes north of the Black Sea, in the Yamna culture. He explains its expansion through mobile herding with wagons and horses, through institutions such as patronage and the oath between guest and host, and through the adoption of the newcomers' language rather than military conquest.

It is the most elaborate version of the steppe hypothesis. The 2015 ancient DNA study, to which Anthony contributed, supported his idea of a large migration from the steppe, though it cannot show what language the migrants spoke. His evidence for early horse riding (the tooth wear at Dereivka and Botai) and his reconstruction of social institutions from linguistics have been disputed. Lazaridis et al. (2022) and Heggarty et al. (2023) instead propose an older homeland south of the Caucasus, with the steppe as a secondary center.

fuentes/migracion-esteparia-haak-2015/ti.texto: Massive migration from the steppe was a source for Indo-European languages in Europe

fuentes/migracion-esteparia-haak-2015/au.texto: Wolfgang Haak, Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, David Reich et al.

fuentes/migracion-esteparia-haak-2015/re.texto: Using whole-genome data from 69 Europeans who lived between 8,000 and 3,000 years ago, the study shows that the early farmers of Germany, Hungary and Spain were closely related to one another and distinct from the local hunter-gatherers; that the Yamna herders descended from hunters of eastern Europe and from a population with Near Eastern ancestry; and that by 2500 BC individuals of the Corded Ware culture in Germany had nearly three-quarters of their ancestry from populations like those of Yamna.

fuentes/migracion-esteparia-haak-2015/po.texto: It was the first major study of ancient DNA in Europe and, together with Allentoft et al. from the same year, supported the steppe hypothesis of the origin of Europe's Indo-European languages. DNA shows ancestry, not languages or identities: the link to Indo-European is an inference by the authors, and the samples were few and uneven. Volker Heyd (“Kossinna's smile,” 2017) and Martin Furholt (2018) warned against returning to the “waves of peoples” of the 20th century and against treating archaeological cultures as homogeneous populations.

fuentes/tres-poblaciones-ancestrales-laz.texto: Ancient human genomes suggest three ancestral populations for present-day Europeans
Iosif Lazaridis, Nick Patterson, Johannes Krause, David Reich et al.

Using the genomes of a farmer from Stuttgart some 7,000 years old and of eight hunter-gatherers from Luxembourg and Sweden, compared with 2,345 present-day people, the study proposes that almost all Europeans descend from three populations: Western hunter-gatherers, “Ancient North Eurasians” related to Upper Paleolithic Siberians, and the first European farmers, whose origins lie mainly in the Near East.
It established the three-component model (hunters, farmers and a third ancestry later identified with the steppe) that all the later studies used.

fuentes/who-we-are-reich/titulo.texto: Who We Are and How We Got Here: Ancient DNA and the New Science of the Human Past

fuentes/who-we-are-reich/resumen.texto: Reich summarizes for the general public what ancient DNA says about human migrations: interbreeding with Neanderthals, the peopling of Europe by hunters, farmers and steppe herders, and the genetic history of India, the Americas and Africa. He argues that almost all present-day populations are mixtures of earlier, very different populations.

fuentes/who-we-are-reich/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most influential popularization of ancient genetics. Anthropologists and archaeologists criticized its generalizations about “peoples” and migrations, its loaded vocabulary and its passages on differences between populations. In 2018, 67 scientists and scholars objected in an open letter (BuzzFeed News) to how it handled race in an opinion piece that previewed the book.

fuentes/corded-ware-kristiansen-2017/tit.texto: Re-theorising mobility and the formation of culture and language among the Corded Ware Culture in Europe

fuentes/corded-ware-kristiansen-2017/aut.texto: Kristian Kristiansen, Morten E. Allentoft et al.

fuentes/corded-ware-kristiansen-2017/res.texto: Kristiansen and colleagues propose that the Corded Ware culture arose when groups of young people from the steppe, mostly men, settled in central Europe and took wives from neighboring farming communities. From that contact came a new culture and a new language, the ancestor of the Germanic, Baltic and Slavic languages.

fuentes/corded-ware-kristiansen-2017/por.texto: It is an attempt to move from DNA to social life and languages. Other archaeologists criticize it for reducing varied processes to a story of warrior bands and for moving too quickly from genes to languages.

fuentes/genomica-de-la-edad-del-bronce-a.texto: Population genomics of Bronze Age Eurasia
Morten E. Allentoft, Martin Sikora, Kristian Kristiansen, Eske Willerslev et al.

Using low-coverage genomes of 101 people from the Bronze Age across Eurasia, from Europe to Siberia, the study describes large-scale migrations and population replacements between 3000 and 1000 BC, among them the genetic kinship of the Corded Ware culture with Yamna. The authors conclude that their data are compatible with the spread of Indo-European languages in the early Bronze Age, and note that light skin was already common but lactose tolerance was not yet.

It appeared in the same volume of Nature as Haak et al. and reached the same conclusion about the steppe by a different route. It received the same criticisms (Heyd 2017, Furholt 2018): that it treats archaeological cultures as peoples and moves from genes to languages without being able to prove that step.

fuentes/arco-sur-lazaridis-2022/titulo.texto: The genetic history of the Southern Arc: A bridge between West Asia and Europe

fuentes/arco-sur-lazaridis-2022/autor.texto: Iosif Lazaridis, Songül Alpaslan-Roodenberg, David Reich et al.

fuentes/arco-sur-lazaridis-2022/resumen.texto: With 727 ancient individuals from Anatolia, southeastern Europe and Western Asia across ten thousand years, the study shows that the ancestry of the Yamna herders formed in the steppe with contributions from the Caucasus, Anatolia and the Levant, and that Anatolia received almost no Yamna ancestry. Since Bronze Age Anatolia, where Hittite and other Anatolian languages were spoken, lacks that ancestry, the authors propose that the homeland of Proto-Indo-Anatolian (the common ancestor of Anatolian and the rest of Indo-European) lay in Western Asia, and that the steppe was a secondary center from which the other branches spread.

fuentes/arco-sur-lazaridis-2022/por_que_.texto: It is the main genetic proposal for a homeland south of the Caucasus, close to those of Gamkrelidze and Ivanov and, in part, to Renfrew's. Its critics note that the lack of steppe ancestry does not prove the absence of a language, which could arrive with few immigrants: Anthony (2007) had already proposed that the ancestors of Anatolian speakers passed through the Balkans in small groups.

fuentes/arbol-de-lenguas-gray-atkinson-2.texto: Language-tree divergence times support the Anatolian theory of Indo-European origin
Russell D. Gray and Quentin D. Atkinson

Applying Bayesian methods from evolutionary biology to a list of basic vocabulary from 87 Indo-European languages, it dates the family's initial split between 7,800 and 9,800 years ago. The authors conclude that this date supports Renfrew's hypothesis of an expansion with agriculture from Anatolia.

It opened the use of Bayesian phylogenetics in historical linguistics. Many linguists objected that it treats word replacement as if it had a measurable rhythm, like the old glottochronology, and Chang et al. (2015) showed that, if ancient languages are treated as ancestors of modern ones, the root comes close to the date of the steppe.

fuentes/filogenia-con-antepasados-chang-.texto: Ancestry-constrained phylogenetic analysis supports the Indo-European steppe hypothesis
Will Chang, Chundra Cathcart, David Hall and Andrew Garrett

It repeats the type of analysis used by Gray and Atkinson, but requires some ancient languages (such as Latin or Vedic Sanskrit) to be direct ancestors of modern ones, as historical linguistics establishes. With that constraint, the root of Indo-European falls around 6,500 years ago, a date compatible with the steppe hypothesis and not with the Anatolian one.

It showed that Bayesian phylogenetic dates depend heavily on their assumptions. Heggarty et al. (2023) responded with a new database that, with sampled ancestors also included, again gives an older root. The debate remains open.

fuentes/hipotesis-hibrida-heggarty-2023/.texto: Language trees with sampled ancestors support a hybrid model for the origin of Indo-European languages
Paul Heggarty, Cormac Anderson, Russell D. Gray et al.

With a new database of basic vocabulary for some 160 Indo-European languages, coded to avoid the inconsistencies of earlier studies, and a Bayesian method that admits ancient languages as ancestors, the study dates the root of the family to about 8,100 years ago. Since that date does not fit the steppe hypothesis, the authors propose a homeland south of the Caucasus, with a later branch moving north into the steppe and from there into Europe, and they reconcile this with the ancient DNA of Lazaridis et al. (2022).

It is the most recent study in the line of Gray and Atkinson (2003), and it gives dates older than the steppe. Defenders of the steppe object to the assumptions behind those dates, which under other criteria (Chang et al., 2015) gave about 6,500 years. The homeland south of the Caucasus, for its part, rests on a genetic reading that also shows no languages.

fuentes/kossinnas-smile-heyd-2017/resume.texto: Heyd, a specialist in Yamna and Corded Ware, accepts that ancient DNA shows a large arrival of steppe ancestry, but criticizes how geneticists tell the story: they equate archaeological cultures with populations, simplify the chronologies and use maps with arrows reminiscent of the methods of Gustaf Kossinna, which is where the title comes from. He also points out that Yamna and Corded Ware have different customs and objects, so the latter does not simply derive from the former.

fuentes/kossinnas-smile-heyd-2017/por_qu.texto: It is one of the most cited archaeological criticisms of the studies by Haak et al. and Allentoft et al., alongside that of Furholt (2018). It does not dispute the genetic data but the step from genes to peoples and languages.

fuentes/migraciones-masivas-furholt-2018.texto: Massive Migrations? The Impact of Recent aDNA Studies on our View of Third Millennium Europe

Furholt argues that the 2015 genetic studies treat archaeological cultures (Yamna, Corded Ware) as homogeneous, closed groups, in the manner of early 20th-century archaeology, and that the same data allow another reading: the sustained mobility of small groups and individuals over centuries, with gradual mixing, rather than a mass invasion.

It is the most systematic archaeological critique of the “massive migrations” narrative. It does not deny the large contribution of steppe ancestry, but questions the scale, the pace and the idea of peoples as units. The usual objection to his reading is that a change of up to three quarters of the ancestry in a few centuries implies, one way or another, the movement of many people.

fuentes/el-fenomeno-campaniforme-olalde-.texto: The Beaker phenomenon and the genomic transformation of northwest Europe
Iñigo Olalde, Selina Brace, Kristian Kristiansen, David Reich et al.

With 400 genomes from the Neolithic, the Copper Age and the Bronze Age, 226 of them associated with Bell Beakers, the study shows that Bell Beaker individuals from the Iberian Peninsula and central Europe had little genetic relationship to one another, so that a fashion, not a people, spread between those regions. The arrival of Bell Beakers in Britain, by contrast, came with a migration that replaced about 90% of the island's ancestry within a few centuries.

It showed that a single archaeological culture could spread sometimes through imitation and sometimes through migration. Some British archaeologists disputed the word “replacement” and the speed of the change. It remains unclear how the replacement happened (violence, epidemics such as plague, or better survival).

fuentes/historia-genomica-de-iberia-olal.texto: The genomic history of the Iberian Peninsula over the past 8000 years
Iñigo Olalde, Swapan Mallick, Nick Patterson, David Reich et al.

With 271 ancient Iberians, the study documents sporadic contacts with North Africa around 2500 BC and, around 2000 BC, the replacement of 40% of the ancestry and of almost all Y chromosomes by people with steppe ancestry. In the Iron Age this ancestry was present both in the regions speaking Indo-European languages and in those speaking Iberian or Vasconic, and present-day Basques resemble a typical Iron Age population without the later admixtures.

It broke the idea of the Basques as an isolated remnant of the Paleolithic or the Neolithic: their language survived despite a large arrival of steppe ancestry, which shows that genes and languages can separate. The interpretation of the replacement of male lineages (violence, prestige, social structure) remains open.

fuentes/neolitico-britanico-brace-2019/t.texto: Ancient genomes indicate population replacement in Early Neolithic Britain

fuentes/neolitico-britanico-brace-2019/a.texto: Selina Brace, Yoan Diekmann, Thomas J. Booth et al.

fuentes/neolitico-britanico-brace-2019/r.texto: With 6 Mesolithic and 67 Neolithic genomes from Britain, the study concludes that farming reached the island around 4000 BC through a migration of farmers related to those of the Iberian Peninsula, which almost completely replaced the local hunter-gatherers.

fuentes/neolitico-britanico-brace-2019/p.texto: It settled an old British debate between adoption and migration in favor of migration. It shows that the builders of the British megaliths, Stonehenge included, descended from those farmers and lived two thousand years or more before any trace of Celtic languages on the island. Which language they spoke is not known.

fuentes/irlanda-neolitica-cassidy-2016/t.texto: Neolithic and Bronze Age migration to Ireland and establishment of the insular Atlantic genome

fuentes/irlanda-neolitica-cassidy-2016/a.texto: Lara M. Cassidy, Daniel G. Bradley et al.

fuentes/irlanda-neolitica-cassidy-2016/r.texto: The first complete genomes of prehistoric Irish people: a Neolithic woman from Ballynahatty (3343–3020 BC), of ancestry mostly from Near Eastern farmers, and three Bronze Age men from Rathlin Island (2026–1534 BC), with a strong steppe inheritance. The authors note that this turnover opens the possibility that an Indo-European language, perhaps an ancestor of Celtic, arrived then.

fuentes/irlanda-neolitica-cassidy-2016/p.texto: It showed that Ireland was not left out of the European migrations, and that the genetic continuity of the Irish goes back to the Bronze Age, not the Neolithic. There are only four individuals; the arrival of Celtic remains a hypothesis, not a result.

fuentes/elite-dinastica-de-newgrange-cas.texto: A dynastic elite in monumental Neolithic society
Lara M. Cassidy, Daniel G. Bradley et al.

With 44 genomes from the Irish Neolithic, the study identifies the man buried in the most elaborate niche at Newgrange as the child of a first-degree incestuous union, something known as a norm only among the elites of divine kings. It also finds distant relatives of his in other large passage tombs.

It is the strongest genetic argument for hierarchy in megalithic societies. Other researchers warn that a single case of incest is not enough to infer a dynasty, and that the reading with medieval Irish myths of kings who marry their sisters, proposed by the authors, is speculative.

fuentes/migracion-a-britania-patterson-2.texto: Large-scale migration into Britain during the Middle to Late Bronze Age

With data from 793 individuals, the study finds that between 1000 and 875 BC the ancestry of the first farmers increased in southern Britain (England and Wales), but not in Scotland, owing to the arrival of migrants genetically similar to the ancient inhabitants of France. These migrants contributed about half of the ancestry of the Iron Age population, which the authors propose as a plausible vehicle for the arrival of the first Celtic languages in Britain.

It added a new data point to the debate on the origin of Celtic. It is compatible with a Celtic that arrived from France in the Late Bronze Age (as Sims-Williams proposes), and hardly compatible with one that arrived in the Iron Age, when the genetic contribution from the continent was smaller. It does not rule out that an Indo-European language, or Celtic itself, had arrived earlier with the Bell Beakers. The relation between that migration and language is an inference by the authors, not a result. David Reich, Ian Armit and dozens of co-authors also sign the paper.

fuentes/galos-de-la-edad-del-hierro-fisc.texto: Origin and mobility of Iron Age Gaulish groups in present-day France revealed through archaeogenomics
Claire-Elise Fischer, Marie-Hélène Pemonge, Mélanie Pruvost et al.

With 49 genomes from Iron Age communities in six regions of France, the study finds no break between the Bronze Age and the Iron Age: the shift to La Tène culture would be a local cultural and economic change, not the mass arrival of a people. The regional groups, although with distinct archaeological cultures, were genetically very homogeneous, owing to mobility among them and exchange with England and the Iberian Peninsula.

It contradicts, like Brunel et al. (2020), the image of “Celtic invasions” as the explanation for the French Iron Age. The authors start from the fact that the Gauls are “usually presented” as direct ancestors of the French. Their data speak of population continuity, not of identities or languages, and 49 individuals from six regions are a small sample for the whole Iron Age.

fuentes/francia-7000-anos-brunel-2020/ti.texto: Ancient genomes from present-day France unveil 7,000 years of its demographic history

fuentes/francia-7000-anos-brunel-2020/au.texto: Samantha Brunel, E. Andrew Bennett, Eva-Maria Geigl, Thierry Grange et al.

fuentes/francia-7000-anos-brunel-2020/re.texto: With mitochondrial genomes, Y-chromosome markers and other data from 243 individuals from present-day France across 7,000 years, plus 58 low-coverage genomes, the study finds what neighboring regions show: an arrival of farmers of Anatolian origin who mixed in varying degrees with local hunters, and a large contribution of people with steppe ancestry at the start of the Bronze Age. It detects no major demographic changes between the Bronze Age and the Iron Age.

fuentes/francia-7000-anos-brunel-2020/po.texto: Together with Fischer et al. (2022), it is the main genetic evidence against a “Celtic invasion” of Iron Age France. It tells us who the ancestors of those people were, not what language they spoke or what they called themselves.

fuentes/celtic-from-the-west/titulo.texto: Celtic from the West: Alternative Perspectives from Archaeology, Genetics, Language and Literature

fuentes/celtic-from-the-west/resumen.texto: Volume edited by Barry Cunliffe and John T. Koch, bringing together archaeologists, geneticists and linguists to argue that Celtic was not born in central Europe with Hallstatt and La Tène, but on the Atlantic seaboard during the Bronze Age, as the language of maritime exchange networks, and that it spread eastward from there. Two further volumes followed (2013 and 2016).

fuentes/celtic-from-the-west/por_que_imp.texto: It opened the largest recent debate on the origin of Celtic. Its critics, above all Patrick Sims-Williams (2012 and 2020), objected that it relies on glottochronology, on misread place-name maps and on the disputed reading of the southwestern inscriptions as Celtic. DNA does not settle the question: Olalde et al. (2018) show a large migration with the Bell Beaker, the moment that the second volume (2013, “Rethinking the Bronze Age and the Arrival of Indo-European in Atlantic Europe”) already discussed as a possible arrival of Indo-European in the Atlantic, and Patterson et al. (2022) document another in the Late Bronze Age, which its authors propose as the most plausible vehicle of Celtic in Britain.

fuentes/tartessian-koch-2009/titulo.texto: Tartessian: Celtic in the South-west at the Dawn of History

fuentes/tartessian-koch-2009/resumen.texto: Koch proposes reading the inscriptions on the stelae of southwestern Iberia (southern Portugal and western Andalusia) as texts in a Celtic language, Tartessian, with funerary formulas that he identifies with Celtic verbs and names. If so, they would be the oldest Celtic texts and would prove Celtic at the far western edge of Europe in the 7th century BC.

fuentes/tartessian-koch-2009/por_que_imp.texto: It is the linguistic basis of the “Celtic from the West” thesis. Most specialists in the ancient languages of Hispania do not accept it: Joseph Eska (review in Kratylos, 2013), Javier de Hoz (who in 2019 called it a “false decipherment”) and Jesús Rodríguez Ramos object that the signs cannot be read with certainty, that the division of words is uncertain, and that the Celtic parallels may be coincidental or loanwords. Only some personal names of apparently Celtic type, already noted by José Antonio Correa (1989) and Jürgen Untermann (1997), have wider acceptance; Terrence Kaufman (2015) considered a Celtic relationship possible.

fuentes/alternativa-de-sims-williams-202.texto: An Alternative to 'Celtic from the East' and 'Celtic from the West'

Sims-Williams criticizes the readings of classical texts and of onomastics that led to “Celtic from the East” (Celts born with the eastern Hallstatt culture), and the fragility of the linguistic evidence for “Celtic from the West”: glottochronology, which assumes that languages change at a steady rate, misinterpreted place-name maps, and the undeciphered inscriptions of southwestern Iberia. He proposes that Celtic radiated from France during the first millennium BC, an explanation he considers more economical.

Patterson et al. (2022) considered it compatible with the migration from France that they detected in the Late Bronze Age. Those who read the southwestern stelae as Celtic reject it, because it implies that there was no Celtic in the Iberian Peninsula before the first millennium BC. The author himself presents it as the most economical explanation, not as a proof.
Article in the Cambridge Archaeological Journal (open access)

fuentes/diccionario-etimologico-del-prot.texto: It reconstructs the roots of Proto-Celtic from Gaulish, Celtiberian, Lepontic and the Insular Celtic languages, with their Indo-European etymologies where there is one. It includes a section on the words with no Indo-European etymology, which may come from earlier languages.

It is the reference work for Proto-Celtic vocabulary, and for dating and locating the language through its words (for agriculture, metal and the sea). Like any etymological dictionary, its entries are debated one by one. Continental Celtic, known from few texts, weighs less than the Insular languages, documented centuries later.

fuentes/ancient-celtic-place-names-sims-.texto: Ancient Celtic Place-Names in Europe and Asia Minor

It gathers the ancient place-names that can be attributed to Celtic (with elements such as -briga, -dunum, nemeto- and -magos), drawn from sources such as Ptolemy, Roman itineraries and inscriptions, and maps them by region with explicit criteria for what is Celtic and what is not.

It is the empirical basis for speaking of where Celtic was spoken in antiquity. Sims-Williams warns that place-names do not date when the language arrived. Supporters of “Celtic from the West” used his maps in another way, a use he himself criticized.

fuentes/the-dawn-of-european-civilizatio.texto: The first synthesis of European prehistory organized by archaeological cultures, each defined by a set of objects, houses and burial customs that recur. Childe explains the spread of agriculture and metallurgy from the Near East by way of the Danube and the Mediterranean, and names cultures such as the “Danubian.”

It fixed the concept of the archaeological culture that was used throughout the 20th century, including for Hallstatt and La Tène. His diffusionism (“ex Oriente lux”) was undone by calibrated radiocarbon dates, which showed that many European monuments predate their supposed Eastern models (Renfrew, 1973).

fuentes/die-herkunft-der-germanen/titulo.texto: The Origin of the Germans: On the Method of Settlement Archaeology

fuentes/die-herkunft-der-germanen/resume.texto: Kossinna sets out his method: the areas of well-defined archaeological cultures always coincide with those of peoples or tribes, so one can trace a people back in time through its objects. With it he places the homeland of the Germans, and of the Indo-Europeans, in northern Germany and Scandinavia.

fuentes/die-herkunft-der-germanen/por_qu.texto: It is the founding text of the equation between cultures and ethnic groups that Nazism used to justify territorial claims. Postwar archaeology rejected it, and criticism of that equation is today the central argument of those who doubt that La Tène is “the culture of the Celts.”

fuentes/manuel-de-archeologie-dechelette.texto: Manual of Prehistoric, Celtic and Gallo-Roman Archaeology

A major synthesis of the prehistory of western Europe, from the Paleolithic to the Roman conquest. The volumes on the Bronze Age, Hallstatt and La Tène order finds from all over Europe with comparative chronologies, and present the La Tène culture as that of the historical Celts of the Greek and Roman texts. The Gallo-Roman part was left unfinished by the author's death in 1914 and was continued by Albert Grenier.

It was the standard reference for half a century and fixed the equation “La Tène = Celts,” which many textbooks still use. Celtic skeptics (Collis, James) criticize it as the origin of the idea of a homogeneous Celtic people identifiable by its objects.
Volume II, part three: La Tène (1914), on Internet Archive

fuentes/early-celtic-art-jacobsthal/resu.texto: A study of the decorated metal objects of the La Tène culture of the 5th and 4th centuries BC. Jacobsthal distinguishes an early style, which transforms Greek and Etruscan palmettes and lotuses and faces of Eastern origin; the Waldalgesheim style, of continuous tendrils; and the plastic and sword styles of the 3rd century BC.

fuentes/early-celtic-art-jacobsthal/por_.texto: His classification still organizes the study of La Tène art. Later researchers (Vincent Megaw, Ruth Megaw, Otto-Herman Frey) discussed the chronology of the styles and his idea of an art born only at the courts of the Rhine and Champagne, and noted that Jacobsthal barely treated insular art.

fuentes/the-ancient-celts-cunliffe/resum.texto: A synthesis of the archaeology of the peoples called Celts, from the Bronze Age to the early Middle Ages: Hallstatt and the princely seats, La Tène and its art, the migrations to Italy, the Balkans and Anatolia, the oppida, the Roman conquest and the Atlantic periphery, with a chapter on the insular traditions. In the second edition (2018) he incorporated the Atlantic thesis and the first genetic data.

fuentes/the-ancient-celts-cunliffe/por_q.texto: It is one of the most widely read books on the subject. Celtic skeptics reproach it for treating as a single people communities that did not call themselves Celtic; others, for taking the stereotypes of the classical authors at face value in its reading of them.

fuentes/facing-the-ocean/titulo.texto: Facing the Ocean: The Atlantic and Its Peoples, 8000 BC-AD 1500

fuentes/facing-the-ocean/resumen.texto: A long-term history of the Atlantic seaboard of Europe, from southern Portugal to Norway, as a region united by the sea: the spread of megalithism, the Atlantic Bronze Age, contacts with Phoenicians and Greeks, and the continuity of routes into the Middle Ages. There Cunliffe begins to propose that Celtic may have formed as a common language of those maritime networks.

fuentes/facing-the-ocean/por_que_importa.texto: It was the direct antecedent of “Celtic from the West.” Its vision of a long-lasting Atlantic identity has been criticized for overstating continuities across millennia.

fuentes/das-grabfeld-von-hallstatt/titul.texto: The Hallstatt Cemetery in Upper Austria and Its Antiquities

fuentes/das-grabfeld-von-hallstatt/resum.texto: The first publication of the cemetery excavated by Johann Georg Ramsauer between 1846 and 1863, with descriptions of nearly a thousand graves, both inhumations and cremations, and plates of its swords, brooches, bronze vessels and ornaments.

fuentes/das-grabfeld-von-hallstatt/por_q.texto: It made known in Europe the material that, a few years later, led Hans Hildebrand to name the “Hallstatt culture.” Like Ramsauer, von Sacken worked with the standards of his time: many grave goods were mixed together, and the internal chronology of the cemetery had to be redone in the 20th century.

fuentes/kingdom-of-salt/titulo.texto: Kingdom of Salt: 7000 Years of Hallstatt

fuentes/kingdom-of-salt/autor.texto: Anton Kern, Kerstin Kowarik, Andreas W. Rausch and Hans Reschreiter (eds.)

fuentes/kingdom-of-salt/resumen.texto: A synthesis by the Natural History Museum in Vienna of research at Hallstatt: salt extraction since the Bronze Age, the galleries with their tools, clothing and wooden ladders preserved, the Iron Age cemetery, and the economy that linked the mine with long-distance trade.

fuentes/kingdom-of-salt/por_que_importa.texto: It brings together the mining archaeology that showed Hallstatt's wealth came from organized industrial extraction. It is an institutional work of scientific outreach by the excavators themselves.

fuentes/heuneburg-fernandez-gotz-krausse.texto: Rethinking Early Iron Age urbanisation in Central Europe: the Heuneburg site and its archaeological environment

It presents recent excavations at the Heuneburg: besides the three-hectare citadel with its mudbrick wall, an outer settlement of some 100 hectares and rich tombs in the surroundings, which show a process of centralization from the late 7th century BC. The authors interpret it as the first stage of urbanization north of the Alps.

It changed the image of the princely seats from isolated chiefs' castles to centers with thousands of inhabitants. Other archaeologists debate whether “urbanization” is the right word for settlements that lasted only a few generations.

fuentes/der-keltenfurst-von-hochdorf/res.texto: The excavator of the Hochdorf tomb describes the 1978–1979 find: the intact wooden chamber, the bronze couch, the wagon, the Greek cauldron with mead residues, the drinking horns, the gold of the dead man and the preserved textiles.

fuentes/der-keltenfurst-von-hochdorf/por.texto: It is the standard publication on the only princely tomb of the Hallstatt period found unlooted. The title “Celtic prince” projects onto the 6th century BC an ethnic label that the texts of the time do not confirm.

fuentes/le-tresor-de-vix/resumen.texto: Publication of the January 1953 find at the foot of Mont Lassois: the intact tomb of a woman with a dismantled wagon, jewelry, a gold torc and the great Greek bronze krater, with Etruscan and Attic vessels for serving wine.

fuentes/le-tresor-de-vix/por_que_importa.texto: It made known the piece that best shows the contact between Hallstatt Gaul and the Greek world. Joffroy interpreted her as a princess; later researchers debated, without agreement, whether she was a ruler, a priestess or a chief's wife.

fuentes/el-enigma-de-los-celtas-del-glau.texto: The Enigma of the Glauberg Celts: Belief, Myth and Reality

The catalog of the exhibition on the Glauberg finds made since 1994: the stone statue of the warrior, the graves in the barrows with their bronze jug and weapons, the processional way and the system of ditches, interpreted as a sanctuary and a place of ancestor worship.
It is the first overall presentation of the site. The astronomical reading of the ditches and the processional way proposed by some of its authors is disputed.

fuentes/la-tene-vouga-1923/titulo.texto: La Tène: Monograph on the Site

fuentes/la-tene-vouga-1923/resumen.texto: The publication of the systematic excavations that Paul Vouga directed at La Tène between 1907 and 1917: the remains of two wooden bridges and of other structures, and thousands of objects (swords with their scabbards, spears, shields, brooches, tools, human remains). Vouga interpreted the site as a military post and proposed dividing La Tène culture into three phases.

fuentes/la-tene-vouga-1923/por_que_impor.texto: It is the main source on the eponymous site. Vouga's interpretation has been replaced by others: a place of weapon offerings in the water, like those at other Celtic sites, or a bridge swept away by a flood with people who were crossing it.

fuentes/megalitos-schulz-paulsson-2019/t.texto: Radiocarbon dates and Bayesian modeling support maritime diffusion model for megaliths in Europe

fuentes/megalitos-schulz-paulsson-2019/r.texto: With 2,410 radiocarbon dates from megalithic, pre-megalithic and contemporary contexts across Europe, the author concludes that megalithic tombs emerged within a span of 200 to 300 years, in the second half of the 5th millennium BC, in northwestern France, the Mediterranean and the Atlantic coast of the Iberian Peninsula, with the oldest focus in northwestern France, and spread by sea in three main phases.

fuentes/megalitos-schulz-paulsson-2019/p.texto: It reopened the debate between a single origin and independent regional origins, dominant since the 1970s. Other specialists objected to the uneven quality of the dates and to the model not explaining why the regional forms are so different.

fuentes/colonizacion-maritima-zilhao-200.texto: Radiocarbon evidence for maritime pioneer colonization at the origins of farming in west Mediterranean Europe

Zilhão discards dates made on unidentified charcoal and uses only those on seeds, shells, domestic animal bones and human remains. With them, the Neolithic “package” appears almost at once from central Italy to Portugal around 5400 BC, within no more than six generations, and he explains it by colonists who advanced by sea.

It was a central argument for migration, rather than adoption of farming by local hunters, which ancient DNA later confirmed for the coast. The model does not say how much the local hunter-gatherers contributed in each region.

fuentes/newgrange-okelly-1982/resumen.texto: The excavator of Newgrange presents the work from 1962 to 1975: the mound, the passage and the cruciform chamber, the stones carved with spirals, the roof-box above the entrance through which the sun enters at the winter solstice, and the later Bronze Age finds. It includes the medieval Irish legends about the site.

fuentes/newgrange-okelly-1982/por_que_im.texto: It is the standard publication on the monument. His reconstruction of the facade with a white quartz wall was criticized by other archaeologists, who think the quartz formed a pavement in front of the entrance.

fuentes/altar-stone-clarke-2024/titulo.texto: A Scottish provenance for the Altar Stone of Stonehenge

fuentes/altar-stone-clarke-2024/autor.texto: Anthony J. I. Clarke, Christopher L. Kirkland, Richard E. Bevins et al.

fuentes/altar-stone-clarke-2024/resumen.texto: Using the age and chemistry of zircon, apatite and rutile grains from the Altar Stone, the great sandstone block lying at the center of Stonehenge, the study shows that it does not come from Wales, as was believed, but from the Orcadian basin in northeastern Scotland, more than 700 km away.

fuentes/altar-stone-clarke-2024/por_que_.texto: It reveals a transport capacity and a network of contacts in Neolithic Britain greater than assumed. It does not resolve how the block was moved, by land or by sea.

fuentes/the-amesbury-archer-fitzpatrick-.texto: The Amesbury Archer and the Boscombe Bowmen: Bell Beaker Burials at Boscombe Down, Amesbury, Wiltshire

Wessex Archaeology's report on the Bell Beaker graves found in 2002 near Stonehenge: that of the archer, with the richest grave goods of the early British Bronze Age, and a nearby collective grave of several men, the “Boscombe Bowmen.” Oxygen and strontium isotopes indicate that the archer grew up in central Europe, probably in the Alpine region.
It is the basis of the image of the Bell Beaker as a phenomenon of traveling people. The isotopes indicate a broad region of origin, not a precise place.

fuentes/genoma-de-otzi-wang-2023/titulo.texto: High-coverage genome of the Tyrolean Iceman reveals unusually high Anatolian farmer ancestry

fuentes/genoma-de-otzi-wang-2023/autor.texto: Ke Wang, Kay Prüfer, Ben Krause-Kyora, Johannes Krause, Albert Zink et al.

fuentes/genoma-de-otzi-wang-2023/resumen.texto: A new high-coverage Ötzi genome, with little contamination, corrects the 2012 one: the man, dated to between 3350 and 3120 BC, had no steppe ancestry and retained the highest proportion of Anatolian farmer ancestry among Europeans of his time, a sign of a fairly isolated Alpine population. He also had darker skin than the usual reconstruction and was probably bald.

fuentes/genoma-de-otzi-wang-2023/por_que.texto: It shows what the population of the Alps was like before the arrival of steppe ancestry, and how a contaminated genome can lead to mistaken conclusions.

fuentes/disco-de-nebra/autor.texto: Bronze Age craftsmen of the Únětice culture

fuentes/disco-de-nebra/resumen.texto: A bronze disk about 30 cm across, with gold inlays representing the Sun or full Moon, a crescent Moon and stars, among them a group of seven usually identified with the Pleiades. Two side arcs would mark the points of sunrise and sunset at the solstices, and another would depict a solar barque. Illegal searchers with metal detectors found it in 1999 on the Mittelberg near Nebra, and the police recovered it in 2002 in Basel.

fuentes/disco-de-nebra/por_que_importa.texto: It is the oldest known concrete representation of the sky, and it has been on UNESCO's Memory of the World register since 2013. In 2020 Rupert Gebhard and Rüdiger Krause argued that the context of the find is not certain and that the disk would date to the Iron Age. Ernst Pernicka, Harald Meller and others responded with analyses of the metal and of the adhering soil, and most specialists maintain the Bronze Age date.

fuentes/etruscos-posth-2021/titulo.texto: The origin and legacy of the Etruscans through a 2000-year archeogenomic time transect

fuentes/etruscos-posth-2021/autor.texto: Cosimo Posth, Valentina Zaro, Johannes Krause, David Caramelli et al.

fuentes/etruscos-posth-2021/resumen.texto: With 82 individuals from Etruria and southern Italy between 800 BC and AD 1000, the study shows that in the Iron Age the Etruscans had steppe ancestry, like their Indo-European-speaking neighbors, and not a recent mixture from Anatolia. Their population as a whole remained stable through the first millennium BC and changed abruptly in the Roman imperial period.

fuentes/etruscos-posth-2021/por_que_impo.texto: It contradicts Herodotus's claim (I.94) that the Etruscans came from Lydia, and shows that a non-Indo-European language survived in a population genetically similar to those that spoke Indo-European languages. It does not explain how or when Etruscan arrived in Italy.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-castelletto-ticin.texto: Inscription on the Castelletto Ticino vessel (“χosioiso”)

A single word written from right to left on the neck of a vessel from a tomb at Castelletto sopra Ticino, on the shore of Lake Maggiore: “χosioiso,” a Celtic genitive interpreted as “of Xosios,” probably an ownership mark (Lexicon Leponticum, NO·1).

Dated to the second quarter of the 6th century BC, it was, when published in 1988, the oldest datable document in a Celtic language. It shows that Celtic was spoken in the Golasecca culture long before the Gaulish invasions of the 4th century BC.
Lexicon Leponticum entry NO·1, with reading, date and bibliography

fuentes/inscripcion-de-prestino/resumen.texto: Slab found at Prestino, near Como, with one line of text in the Lugano alphabet: “uvamokozis : plialeθu : uvltiauiopos : ariuonepos : siteś : tetu.” It is interpreted as a dedication: a certain Uvamokozis “gave” (tetu) some seats or a monument (siteś) to recipients named in the plural (uvltiauiopos, ariuonepos). The Lexicon Leponticum (CO·48) dates it to the second quarter of the 5th century BC.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-prestino/por_que_.texto: It is the longest Lepontic inscription and the one that best proves Lepontic is a Celtic language, based on its grammar and verb forms. The translation of several words is still under discussion.

fuentes/inscripcion-de-prestino/leer.0.t.texto: Lexicon Leponticum entry CO·48, with reading, date and bibliography

fuentes/lexicon-leponticum/resumen.texto: Online corpus and dictionary of the Celtic inscriptions of pre-Roman Italy (Lepontic and Cisalpine Gaulish), directed by David Stifter with Corinna Salomon and others at the University of Vienna. Each inscription has its own entry with the object, reading, date, bibliography and analysis of the words.

fuentes/lexicon-leponticum/por_que_impor.texto: It is the open, up-to-date reference source for the oldest Celtic writing. Its dates and readings reflect the state of research and are corrected when new data appear.

fuentes/estelas-del-suroeste/resumen.texto: About 95 inscriptions carved on stone slabs, mostly in the Algarve and Lower Alentejo and some in Extremadura and western Andalusia, in a semisyllabic script derived from Phoenician, the oldest on the peninsula. Many turned up in Early Iron Age necropolises and are usually dated to the 7th century BC.

fuentes/estelas-del-suroeste/por_que_imp.texto: They are the center of the debate over Tartessian. John T. Koch (since 2009) reads them as Celtic, and Terrence Kaufman (2015) considered this possible, while Javier de Hoz, Joseph Eska and Jesús Rodríguez Ramos regard them as undeciphered and unclassified, with at most a few Celtic personal names, as Correa (1989) and Untermann (1997) had already noted. Most of the slabs were found out of their original context; the most secure date is that of the Medellín inscription, around 650-625 BC.

fuentes/plomo-de-alcoy/titulo.texto: Lead plaque from Alcoy (La Serreta I)

fuentes/plomo-de-alcoy/resumen.texto: Lead sheet found in 1921 at the Iberian sanctuary and settlement of La Serreta, in Alcoy, with several texts written in Iberian using adapted Greek letters (the Greco-Iberian alphabet). Because it is written in a known script, it can be read with certainty, although its content, perhaps commercial, is not understood.

fuentes/plomo-de-alcoy/por_que_importa.texto: Manuel Gómez-Moreno published it in 1922 and used it, together with the coins, to fix the values of the Iberian script. It is one of the longest Iberian texts.

fuentes/monumenta-linguarum-hispanicarum.texto: Corpus of all the pre-Roman inscriptions of the Iberian Peninsula and southern France: the coin legends (1975), the Iberian inscriptions of France (1980) and of Spain (1990), and the Celtiberian, Lusitanian and southwestern ones (1997), with their reading, date and analysis.

It is the basis of all study of the Paleohispanic languages. Its classifications (Lusitanian as Indo-European, not necessarily Celtic; Tartessian unclassified) are the ones the Atlantic thesis discusses.

fuentes/mano-de-irulegi/soporte.texto: Bronze plaque in the shape of a hand

fuentes/mano-de-irulegi/resumen.texto: Bronze plaque in the shape of an outstretched right hand, found in 2021 at an Iron Age settlement at the foot of the Irulegi castle (Navarre), which was destroyed in the Sertorian wars of the 1st century BC. It has a short inscription in northeastern Iberian script on the back. It was presented in November 2022.

fuentes/mano-de-irulegi/por_que_importa.texto: Joaquín Gorrochategui and Javier Velaza read it as the oldest text in a Vasconic language, an ancestor of Basque, and proposed that its first word, “sorioneku,” corresponds to Basque “zorioneko” (“of good fortune”). Other linguists dispute that reading, and the text, as the find record itself notes, cannot be translated.

fuentes/onomastica-indigena-de-aquitania.texto: Study of the nearly four hundred non-Latin personal and divine names in the Roman inscriptions of Aquitania and the Pyrenees. Gorrochategui separates those of Celtic origin from those of the Aquitanians and shows that the latter are explained by an older form of Basque (for example, Nescato, Cison, Andere).
It is the standard study of Aquitanian and the firmest evidence that a Vasconic language was spoken north of the Pyrenees in Roman times. Only names are known, not sentences.

fuentes/fonetica-historica-vasca/resumen.texto: Mitxelena reconstructs, with the comparative method, the history of Basque sounds from an earlier common language, Proto-Basque. He compares dialects, medieval texts, Latin loanwords and the Aquitanian names of Roman times.

fuentes/fonetica-historica-vasca/por_que.texto: He founded historical Basque linguistics and, on methodological grounds, rejected many comparisons of Basque with other languages (Iberian, Caucasian, Berber). His Proto-Basque is the starting point of all serious discussion of the pre-Indo-European languages of western Europe.

fuentes/laminas-de-pyrgi/resumen.texto: Three gold sheets found in 1964 in the sanctuary of Pyrgi, the port of Caere, with a dedication by Thefarie Velianas, ruler of Caere, to the goddess Uni, identified with the Phoenician Astarte: two texts in Etruscan and one in Phoenician that says almost the same thing.

fuentes/laminas-de-pyrgi/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most important bilingual text for understanding Etruscan, and evidence of the alliance between Etruscans and Carthaginians that Herodotus mentions for the battle of Alalia.

fuentes/liber-linteus/resumen.texto: The longest surviving Etruscan text, written in a linen book that in Ptolemaic Egypt was cut into strips to wrap a mummy. Bought in Alexandria in 1848, it has been in the Archaeological Museum in Zagreb since 1867. From the words that are understood, it seems to be a ritual calendar with offerings to various gods.

fuentes/liber-linteus/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only surviving linen book from antiquity and a central source on Etruscan religion. Since the language is only partly understood, a complete translation is impossible.

fuentes/inscripciones-reticas/soporte.texto: Graffiti on pottery, bone, bronze and stone

fuentes/inscripciones-reticas/resumen.texto: About 280 short inscriptions from the 6th to the 1st centuries BC, found in northern Italy, southern Germany, eastern Switzerland, Austria and Slovenia, written in two variants of North Italic alphabets derived from Etruscan. They are mostly names and dedications on votive objects.

fuentes/inscripciones-reticas/por_que_im.texto: They are the only direct evidence of the language of the Raetians, Alpine neighbors of the Celts, which most specialists regard as related to Etruscan. The online corpus of the University of Vienna (Thesaurus Inscriptionum Raeticarum) gathers them.

fuentes/inscripciones-reticas/leer.0.tit.texto: Thesaurus Inscriptionum Raeticarum, University of Vienna

fuentes/ratisch-und-etruskisch-rix-1998/.texto: Rix compares the grammar of Raetic with that of Etruscan and that of the Lemnos stele, in the Aegean, and concludes that they are three languages of a single family, which he calls Tyrsenian, unrelated to the Indo-European languages.

It is the proposal most scholars accept on the relationship of Etruscan. Some linguists consider the Raetic and Lemnian data too scarce to establish a family, although no one has proposed a solid alternative.

fuentes/tabula-de-polcevera/resumen.texto: Bronze sheet recording the ruling of two arbiters of the Roman Senate, the brothers Quintus and Marcus Minucius Rufus, in a boundary dispute between the city of Genua and the Ligurian community of the Viturii Langenses. It was found in 1506 in the Polcevera valley, north of Genoa.

fuentes/tabula-de-polcevera/por_que_impo.texto: It is one of the few complete legal documents of the Roman Republic and one of the main sources on the Ligurians, because it names mountains, streams and places in their territory. Those names feed the debate over the Ligurian language: some have Indo-European and perhaps Celtic endings, others cannot be explained, and linguists do not agree on whether it was an Indo-European language.

fuentes/unsere-altesten-flussnamen/resum.texto: Krahe gathers river names spread from Scandinavia and the Baltic to the Iberian Peninsula and Britain, formed from a small group of roots and suffixes (such as *al-, *sal-, *var-, -nt-) that he relates to water and to Indo-European. He assigns them to an “Old European” language, earlier than the separation of Celtic, Germanic, Italic, Illyrian and Baltic.

fuentes/unsere-altesten-flussnamen/por_q.texto: It is the founding study of Paleo-European hydronymy. Its critics (such as Peter Kitson) object that the roots are so short that the matches may be chance. Wolfgang P. Schmid reinterpreted it with a focus on the Baltic, and Theo Vennemann read it as non-Indo-European.

fuentes/europa-vasconica-europa-semitica.texto: Gathers the articles in which Vennemann argues that the oldest river and place names of Europe, including Krahe's, come from a “Vasconic” family of languages related to Basque, spoken since the Mesolithic. He also argues that Semitic-speaking peoples who arrived by the Atlantic left traces in the vocabulary and syntax of Germanic and insular Celtic.

It is the best-known version of a minority thesis on the languages before the Indo-European ones. Philip Baldi and B. Richard Page (Lingua, 2006) and the Basque scholar Larry Trask rejected his etymologies as arbitrary, for comparing with modern Basque rather than with the Proto-Basque reconstructed by Mitxelena, and for not applying the comparative method. Vennemann partly based his thesis on the genetics of the 1990s, which saw the Basques as remnants of the people who resettled Europe after the last glaciation. Ancient DNA did not confirm that picture (Olalde 2019), although genes alone do not decide which language was spoken.

personas/argantonio/resumen.texto: King of Tartessos who, according to Herodotus (I.163), reigned eighty years, lived one hundred and twenty, received the Phocaeans in friendship and gave them money to wall their city against the Persians. He is the first king of the Iberian Peninsula whose name is known outside legend. Such a long life is probably an exaggeration or the sum of several reigns. His name is usually related to the Celtic *arganto- (“silver”), one of the arguments in the debate over the language of Tartessos.

personas/coleo-de-samos/resumen.texto: Navigator from Samos who, according to Herodotus (IV.152), was blown off course by a storm beyond the Pillars of Heracles around 640 BC and reached Tartessos, a port the Greeks did not yet frequent. He returned from there with a cargo of silver that made him rich. With a tenth of the profit he dedicated to the sanctuary of Hera on Samos a large bronze cauldron with griffin heads. Some historians suspect that the storm in the story conceals a trade route that was meant to be kept secret; this is a conjecture.

personas/christian-jurgensen-thomsen/res.texto: Danish antiquarian who, while arranging the collections of the Copenhagen museum, proposed the three-age system (Stone, Bronze and Iron Ages), published in the museum guide of 1836. That scheme is the basis of all periodizations of European prehistory.

personas/johann-georg-ramsauer/resumen.texto: Director of the Hallstatt salt mines who, between 1846 and 1863, excavated nearly a thousand graves of the prehistoric cemetery on the upper valley. His records, with watercolors of each grave and its objects, were not published in his lifetime, but they remain the main source on that cemetery, from which the Hallstatt culture takes its name. He excavated with the methods of his time: the objects were divided among museums and collectors, and many contexts were lost.

personas/hans-hildebrand/resumen.texto: Swedish archaeologist and historian, antiquary of the kingdom, who in the 1870s proposed dividing the Iron Age of central Europe into two phases, Hallstatt and La Tène, after their eponymous sites. The division is still in use. Its equivalence with a people, the Celts, was a later addition by other authors.

personas/oscar-montelius/resumen.texto: Swedish archaeologist who refined the typological method for dating objects by the evolution of their forms, and who divided the Northern Bronze Age into six periods. His chronology, tied to those of Egypt and Mesopotamia by chains of comparisons, dominated until radiocarbon corrected it for the earliest periods.

personas/otto-tischler/resumen.texto: Prehistorian from Königsberg, in East Prussia, who in 1885 divided La Tène culture into three phases (early, middle and late) according to the form of brooches, swords and scabbards. His scheme is the basis of later Iron Age chronologies. It also influenced the young Gustaf Kossinna.

personas/gustaf-kossinna/resumen.texto: German philologist and prehistorian who formulated “settlement archaeology”: the area of an archaeological culture would be that of a people. With this method he placed the cradle of the Germanic peoples in northern Germany and Scandinavia (“Die Herkunft der Germanen,” 1911). The Nazis used his ideas, and postwar archaeology rejected the automatic equation between cultures and peoples, which also weighs on the equation “La Tène = Celts.”

personas/joseph-dechelette/resumen.texto: French archaeologist, excavator of Bibracte with his uncle Jacques-Gabriel Bulliot, and author of the “Manual of Prehistoric, Celtic and Gallo-Roman Archaeology” (1908–1914), the first major synthesis of the prehistory of western Europe. He identified La Tène culture with the Celts of the ancient authors, an equivalence that dominated the 20th century and is now debated. He died at the front in October 1914, at the start of the First World War.

personas/paul-reinecke/resumen.texto: German prehistorian with the Bavarian monuments service who, between 1902 and 1911, built the chronology still used in central Europe: Bronze A–D, Hallstatt A–D and La Tène A–D. With it, the graves and deposits of different regions could be compared with one another.

personas/paul-jacobsthal/resumen.texto: German classical archaeologist of Jewish origin, professor at Marburg, who left Germany in 1935 because of Nazi persecution and continued his career at Oxford. “Early Celtic Art” (1944) classified La Tène art into styles (early, Waldalgesheim, plastic and of the swords) and showed its Greek, Etruscan and Eastern loans. His scheme remains the basis for the study of that art, although its limits and chronology are debated.

personas/v-gordon-childe/resumen.texto: Australian archaeologist who worked in Edinburgh and London. In “The Dawn of European Civilization” (1925) he ordered European prehistory by archaeological cultures and by diffusion from the East. In “The Aryans” (1926) he placed the Indo-Europeans on the steppe, a book he later disowned because of the racist use made of the topic. A Marxist, he rejected the racial burden of Kossinna's work, although he took over his concept of culture.

personas/rene-joffroy/resumen.texto: French archaeologist who excavated Mont Lassois and, in January 1953 with Maurice Moisson, discovered the Vix grave with its great Greek krater. He published the find in “The Treasure of Vix” (1954) and afterwards directed the Museum of National Antiquities at Saint-Germain-en-Laye.

personas/michael-j-okelly/resumen.texto: Irish archaeologist at University College Cork who excavated Newgrange between 1962 and 1975 and in 1967 verified that the light of the winter solstice sunrise enters through an opening above the doorway and reaches the back of the chamber. His reconstruction of the white quartz facade was disputed by other archaeologists, who doubt the monument looked like that in the Neolithic.

personas/marija-gimbutas/resumen.texto: Lithuanian archaeologist who emigrated to the United States in 1949 and taught at the University of California, Los Angeles. From 1956 she put forward the Kurgan hypothesis: herders from the Pontic steppe would have brought Indo-European languages to Europe in three waves, between around 4400 and 2800 BC. She also described a peaceful, egalitarian Neolithic “Old Europe” centered on the worship of a goddess. That idea was taken up by spiritual feminism and criticized by archaeologists such as Lynn Meskell and Ruth Tringham, who read the figurines as mother goddesses without evidence. Genetic studies of 2015 confirmed a large arrival of steppe ancestry around 3000–2500 BC, close to her last wave, but not the earlier ones or the violence she proposed, and they say nothing about her Old Europe.

personas/colin-renfrew/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, professor at Cambridge, who used calibrated radiocarbon to dismantle the idea that prehistoric Europe copied everything from the East (“Before Civilization,” 1973). In “Archaeology and Language” (1987) he proposed that Indo-European languages arrived with the first farmers from Anatolia around 7000 BC, and that Celtic formed in the west without invasions. Linguists objected that the common vocabulary of the wheel and the chariot cannot be so old. Genetic studies of 2015 instead supported a migration from the steppe, and Renfrew later accepted that migration for Europe, although he kept a more remote Anatolian origin. He died in 2024.

personas/j-p-mallory/resumen.texto: American archaeologist based in Northern Ireland, emeritus professor at Queen's University Belfast. “In Search of the Indo-Europeans” (1989) is the standard synthesis in favor of a steppe origin for those languages. In “The Origins of the Irish” (2013) he reviewed how and when a Celtic language could have reached Ireland, and concluded that the evidence does not allow the question to be settled.

personas/david-w-anthony/resumen.texto: American archaeologist at Hartwick College, a specialist in the steppes of Ukraine and Russia. In “The Horse, the Wheel and Language” (2007) he updated the steppe hypothesis: Proto-Indo-European would have been spoken in the Yamnaya culture and spread with the wagon and the horse. His arguments for early horse domestication were disputed by other specialists, but the genetic studies of 2015, to which he contributed, supported the core of his thesis.

personas/kristian-kristiansen/resumen.texto: Danish archaeologist at the University of Gothenburg, a specialist in the Bronze Age, who collaborated with geneticists on the large studies of ancient DNA. In 2017 he proposed that the Corded Ware culture arose from men who came from the steppe and took wives from neighboring farming groups, a reading that other archaeologists consider a simplification of more varied processes.

personas/barry-cunliffe/resumen.texto: British archaeologist, professor of European archaeology at Oxford between 1972 and 2007, and excavator of the hillfort of Danebury and the Roman villa of Fishbourne. His syntheses (“The Ancient Celts,” 1997; “Facing the Ocean,” 2001) moved from explaining the Celts from Hallstatt and La Tène to stressing the Atlantic façade. With John T. Koch he promoted the thesis “Celtic from the West” (2010). “Celtic skeptics,” such as John Collis and Simon James, reproach him for still using “Celt” as a people label. Linguists such as Patrick Sims-Williams reproach him for relying on disputed readings of Tartessian.

personas/john-t-koch/resumen.texto: American Celticist at the Centre for Advanced Welsh and Celtic Studies of the University of Wales, and editor of the encyclopedia “Celtic Culture” (2006). He argues that Celtic formed on the Atlantic façade during the Bronze Age, and that the southwestern stelae of the Iberian Peninsula are written in a Celtic language, Tartessian (“Tartessian,” 2009). Most specialists do not accept this. Joseph Eska, Javier de Hoz (who called it a “false decipherment”) and Patrick Sims-Williams object that the inscriptions are not securely deciphered.

personas/patrick-sims-williams/resumen.texto: British Celticist at Aberystwyth University, author of “Ancient Celtic Place-Names in Europe and Asia Minor” (2006), which maps ancient Celtic place names. In 2020 he criticized both “Celtic from the East” and “Celtic from the West,” and proposed that Celtic radiated from France in the first millennium BC. Patterson and others (2022) considered that scenario compatible with the migration their genetic study detected.

personas/ranko-matasovic/resumen.texto: Croatian linguist at the University of Zagreb, author of the “Etymological Dictionary of Proto-Celtic” (2009), the reference work on the Proto-Celtic lexicon. He pointed out a group of Celtic words with no Indo-European etymology, a possible trace of earlier languages.

personas/david-reich/resumen.texto: American geneticist at Harvard University whose laboratory produced much of the ancient genomes of Europe (Haak 2015, Olalde 2018 and 2019, Patterson 2022). He summarized those results for the general public in “Who We Are and How We Got Here” (2018). Part of archaeology criticizes him for treating cultures as migrating peoples, as early-20th-century archaeology did, and for an unequal collaboration with those who excavated the remains. The debate reached the press in 2019.

personas/nick-patterson/resumen.texto: British mathematician, formerly a cryptographer in the British signals intelligence service, who turned to population genetics at the Broad Institute and developed with David Reich much of the statistical methods for ancient DNA. He was first author of the 2022 study that detected a large migration from France to southern Britain between 1000 and 875 BC.

personas/inigo-olalde/resumen.texto: Basque geneticist, first author of the studies on the Bell Beaker phenomenon (2018) and on the genomic history of the Iberian Peninsula (2019), both carried out in David Reich's laboratory. He showed that the Bell Beaker expansion replaced some 90% of the ancestry of Britain, and that present-day Basques descend from an Iron Age population that already had steppe ancestry but kept a non-Indo-European language.

personas/hans-krahe/resumen.texto: German linguist at the University of Tübingen who studied the oldest river names of Europe. He called “Old European” (Alteuropäisch) a layer of Indo-European-rooted hydronyms spread from Scandinavia to the Iberian Peninsula, earlier than the separation of Celtic, Germanic, Italic and Baltic. That layer is still debated: Wolfgang P. Schmid centered it on the Baltic, and Theo Vennemann read it as non-Indo-European.

personas/theo-vennemann/resumen.texto: German linguist at the University of Munich. He argues that before the Indo-Europeans, a “Vasconic” family related to Basque was spoken across much of Europe, leaving river and place names, and that Semitic-speaking peoples who arrived by the Atlantic influenced Germanic and insular Celtic (“Europa Vasconica – Europa Semitica,” 2003). Basque specialists and Indo-Europeanists such as Larry Trask, Philip Baldi and Richard Page rejected his etymologies as arbitrary, and his thesis is a minority view in the discipline.

personas/helmut-rix/resumen.texto: German linguist at the University of Freiburg, a specialist in Etruscan and the Italic languages. In “Raetic and Etruscan” (1998) he grouped Etruscan, Raetic and the language of the Lemnos stele into a non-Indo-European family, Tyrsenian.

personas/koldo-mitxelena/resumen.texto: Basque linguist (Luis Michelena in Spanish) who, in “Historical Basque Phonetics” (1961), reconstructed Proto-Basque with the comparative method and showed that the personal and divine names in the Latin inscriptions of Aquitania correspond to an older form of Basque. He was also a central figure in the unification of written Basque.

personas/manuel-gomez-moreno/resumen.texto: Archaeologist and art historian from Granada who, between 1922 and 1925, deciphered the Iberian script by recognizing that it mixed syllabic and alphabetic signs. Since then Iberian can be read, though it is still not understood.

personas/jurgen-untermann/resumen.texto: German linguist at the University of Cologne who gathered the pre-Roman inscriptions of the Iberian Peninsula and southern France in the “Monumenta Linguarum Hispanicarum” (1975–1997). He classified Lusitanian as an Indo-European language and left the language of the southwestern stelae unclassified, although he noted in them some names of apparently Celtic type.

personas/javier-de-hoz/resumen.texto: Spanish linguist at the Complutense University of Madrid, a specialist in Paleohispanic languages and scripts, and author of a “Linguistic History of the Iberian Peninsula in Antiquity” (2010–2011). Among other things, he rejected the reading of the southwestern inscriptions as Celtic.

personas/joaquin-gorrochategui/resumen.texto: Basque linguist at the University of the Basque Country, author of “Indigenous Onomastics of Aquitania” (1984), the standard study of Aquitanian. In 2022, with Javier Velaza, he presented the reading of the Irulegi hand as a text in a Vasconic language.

personas/david-stifter/resumen.texto: Austrian Celticist, professor at Maynooth University, one of those responsible for the Lexicon Leponticum, the online corpus of the Celtic inscriptions of Italy, and author of a grammar of Old Irish (“Sengoídelc,” 2006).

hechos/llegada-de-la-agricultura-a-europ.texto: The first farmers arrive in Europe

From Anatolia and the Aegean, groups of farmers with wheat, barley, sheep and goats spread through Greece and the Balkans by around 6500 BC. They continued along the Danube and the Mediterranean coast, and reached Britain and Ireland by around 4000 BC. Ancient DNA (Lazaridis 2014, Haak 2015, Brace 2019) shows that it was mainly a migration of people and not only of techniques, with variable mixing with the local hunter-gatherers. It is not known what languages they spoke: they left no writing, and the hypotheses range from languages related to those of Anatolia (non-Indo-European, except for Renfrew's) to remnants in Basque and in place names, all without evidence.

hechos/cultura-de-la-ceramica-cardial/re.texto: The first farmers of the western Mediterranean coast, from Italy to Portugal, who decorated their pottery with the edge of the cockle shell (Cardium). João Zilhão (2001) showed that the most reliable dates cluster around 5400 BC along the whole coast, and explained it by colonists who advanced by sea within a few generations. Ancient DNA confirmed that they descended from farmers who had come from the Aegean.

hechos/cultura-de-la-ceramica-de-bandas/.texto: The first agricultural culture of central Europe, with large long wooden houses and pottery decorated with incised bands. It spread within a few centuries from Hungary to the Paris Basin and Ukraine. Childe called it “Danubian I.” Ancient DNA shows that its bearers descended from the farmers of Anatolia. The mass graves of Talheim and Schöneck-Kilianstädten, from around 5000 BC, show that its end involved episodes of violence.

hechos/cultura-de-vinca/resumen.texto: Neolithic culture of the central Balkans, with villages of adobe houses on mounds, clay figurines and early copper metallurgy. Its vessels and tablets bear repeated signs (“Vinča signs”) that Marija Gimbutas and others read as a writing system. Most specialists regard them as marks or symbols with no linguistic value, because they do not form sequences that look like text.

hechos/cultura-de-cucuteni-trypillia/res.texto: Farmers of Moldova and Ukraine who, by around 4000 BC, built the largest villages of their time in Europe, with thousands of houses, and who periodically burned their settlements. For Gimbutas it was the best example of her peaceful “Old Europe,” destroyed by the steppe herders. Anthony, by contrast, describes centuries of contact and exchange with them.

hechos/megalitismo-atlantico/resumen.texto: Collective tombs, menhirs and stone circles were built over some two thousand years, from the south of the Iberian Peninsula to Scandinavia. Bettina Schulz Paulsson (2019), with 2,410 radiocarbon dates, concluded that they originated in northwestern France in the second half of the 5th millennium BC and spread by sea. Other researchers maintain independent regional origins. They have no connection with the Celts or the druids, to whom they were attributed from the 17th century onward.

hechos/alineamientos-de-carnac/resumen.texto: The Neolithic farmers of southern Brittany raised more than three thousand standing stones in rows, in several stages, along with dolmens and mounds such as that of Saint-Michel. Their purpose (ritual, astronomical or assembly) is still unknown.

hechos/construccion-de-newgrange/resumen.texto: A Neolithic community raised in the Boyne valley a mound some 85 m in diameter, with a passage aligned to the sunrise of the winter solstice, surrounded by carved stones with spirals. Michael O'Kelly excavated it between 1962 and 1975. In 2020, Lara Cassidy and her team found that the man buried in its main chamber was the child of a first-degree incestuous union, which they interpret as a sign of a dynastic elite, comparable to the divine kingships of Egypt or the Incas.

hechos/construccion-de-stonehenge/resume.texto: The dates of its phases are approximate. Around 3000 BC a circular ditch with a bank was dug and, according to Mike Parker Pearson and his team, bluestones from the Preseli Hills in Wales were already placed in the Aubrey holes. Around 2500 BC the large sandstone blocks (sarsens) and the trilithons were raised, and the bluestones were rearranged several times until around 1500 BC. In 2024, Anthony Clarke and his team showed that the Altar Stone came from northeastern Scotland, more than 700 km away. The idea of a Druidic temple is an invention of the antiquaries of the 17th and 18th centuries, such as William Stukeley. The monument is two thousand years older than any Celt in Britain.

hechos/muerte-de-otzi/resumen.texto: A man of the Copper Age died on a pass in the Ötztal Alps, on today's border between Austria and Italy, with an arrowhead lodged in his shoulder. His body was preserved in the ice until two hikers found it in 1991. He carried a copper axe, a bow, arrows and clothing of leather and fur. His complete genome (Wang and others, 2023) has no steppe ancestry: it derives mostly from farmers of Anatolian origin, a portrait of the Alpine population before the arrival of steppe ancestry.

hechos/cultura-de-yamna/resumen.texto: Mobile herders of the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas, who used solid-wheeled wagons, kept livestock, and buried some of their dead under mounds (kurgans). For Anthony and Mallory they spoke Proto-Indo-European or a close form. Ancient DNA (Haak 2015) shows that their ancestry arrived en masse in central Europe shortly afterward, although genes are not languages and the link to language is an inference.

hechos/expansion-de-las-lenguas-indoeuro.texto: The spread of the Indo-European languages in Europe

Almost all the languages of Europe descend from Proto-Indo-European, reconstructed by comparative linguistics since the 19th century. Gimbutas (from 1956), Mallory (1989) and Anthony (2007) placed its homeland on the Pontic steppe and its expansion between the 5th and 3rd millennia BC. Renfrew (1987) tied it to the first farmers of Anatolia, some 3,000 years earlier, and linguistic phylogeny gave dates that support one or the other (Gray and Atkinson 2003; Chang and others 2015). The ancient DNA studies of 2015 (Haak, Allentoft) detected a large arrival of steppe ancestry in central Europe in the first half of the 3rd millennium BC, which tipped the discussion in favor of the steppe. Lazaridis and others (2022) and Heggarty and others (2023) propose an earlier homeland in the southern Caucasus, with the steppe as a secondary focus. Archaeologists such as Heyd (2017) and Furholt (2018) warn that DNA shows movements of people, not languages or identities, and that archaeological cultures are not peoples.

hechos/cultura-de-la-ceramica-cordada/re.texto: Culture of central and northern Europe, from the Rhine to the Volga, with vessels decorated with cord impressions, battle-axes and individual graves under mounds, with men lying on their right side and women on their left. Haak and others (2015) found that nearly three quarters of the ancestry of the individuals they analyzed from Germany came from populations like those of Yamnaya. It is usually linked to the ancestors of the Germanic, Baltic and Slavic languages, an inference without texts. Kristiansen and others (2017) proposed that it arose from men from the steppe who took local wives, and Heyd (2017) and Furholt (2018) objected that Corded Ware is not a copy of Yamnaya and that its formation was more gradual and varied.

hechos/fenomeno-campaniforme/resumen.texto: A set of inverted bell-shaped vessels, copper daggers, archer's bracers and buttons spread from around 2750 BC across western and central Europe. Olalde and others (2018) showed that in the Iberian Peninsula and in central Europe different populations carried it, so that it was fashion, not people, that moved between them. But its arrival in Britain came with a migration that replaced some 90% of the island's ancestry within a few centuries. In the Iberian Peninsula, around 2000 BC, people with steppe ancestry had already replaced about 40% of the ancestry and almost all Y chromosomes (Olalde 2019). Non-Indo-European languages such as Iberian and Basque survived there, however: genetic change is not enough to know which language arrived.

hechos/arquero-de-amesbury/resumen.texto: A Bell Beaker grave found in 2002 about 5 km from Stonehenge, the richest of the Early Bronze Age in Britain, with flint arrowheads, archer's bracers, copper knives and the oldest gold objects in England. Isotope analysis of his teeth indicates that the man, aged between 35 and 45, had grown up in the Alpine region of central Europe. It is the clearest individual evidence of the journeys that accompanied the Bell Beaker phenomenon.

hechos/cultura-de-unetice/resumen.texto: Early Bronze Age culture of central Europe, from Bohemia to Saxony, with bronze metallurgy, hoards of axes and ingots, and princely graves under mounds such as those of Leubingen and Helmsdorf. The Nebra sky disk is attributed to it.

hechos/cultura-de-los-tumulos/resumen.texto: Middle Bronze Age culture of central Europe, from eastern France to Hungary, which buried its dead under earth mounds with swords, jewelry and bronze pins. Part of the research took it to be the culture of the ancestors of the Celts, Italics and Illyrians, an assignment of languages that cannot be verified.

hechos/minas-de-sal-de-hallstatt/titulo.texto: The prehistoric salt mines of Hallstatt

hechos/minas-de-sal-de-hallstatt/resumen.texto: In the upper Hallstatt valley, galleries were excavated to extract rock salt from the Bronze Age onward. A wooden staircase dated by dendrochronology to the 14th century BC was found there. The salt preserved tools, torches, clothing, leather baskets and the miners' excrement, which show an organized exploitation that continued into the Iron Age. The wealth of the graves in the neighboring cemetery comes from that salt trade.

hechos/cultura-de-los-campos-de-urnas/re.texto: From around 1300 BC, much of central Europe began to cremate its dead and bury the ashes in urns in large cemeteries, with fortified settlements, bronze armor, and hoards of objects in rivers and marshes. During the 20th century many considered it the culture of the Proto-Celts. Today it is seen more as a change of customs that spread among peoples speaking different languages, although some authors still place the formation of Celtic in that world.
