hechos/bronce-atlantico/resumen.texto: A maritime exchange network that linked the coasts of Portugal, Galicia, France, Britain and Ireland in the Late Bronze Age, with carp's-tongue swords, cauldrons, roasting spits and bronze meat hooks of common types. The Huelva estuary hoard, from around 900 BC, brings together hundreds of pieces. Cunliffe and Koch see in that network the setting in which Celtic spread. Patterson and others (2022) documented a migration from France to southern Britain between 1000 and 875 BC.

hechos/llegada-del-hierro-a-europa-centr.texto: Arrival of iron metallurgy in central Europe

The technique of smelting iron ore, known in Anatolia and the eastern Mediterranean, spread through Greece and Italy and reached north of the Alps around the 8th century BC, when the start of the Hallstatt culture (Hallstatt C) is fixed. Iron, abundant in many places, made tools and weapons cheaper and reduced the value of the copper and tin trade networks.

hechos/cultura-de-hallstatt/resumen.texto: Culture of the early Iron Age of central Europe, from eastern France to Slovenia and Austria, in phases C (around 800-620 BC) and D (around 620-450 BC) of Reinecke's chronology. Phases A and B correspond to the Urnfield culture. It is marked by long iron and bronze swords, four-wheeled funerary wagons and elite graves under large mounds. Its name comes from the cemetery next to the Hallstatt salt mines. Archaeologists such as Déchelette took it to be the cradle of the Celts, because Herodotus (II.33) places the “keltoi” near the sources of the Danube, although the same passages also place them beyond the Pillars of Heracles.

hechos/excavaciones-de-hallstatt/resumen.texto: Johann Georg Ramsauer, director of the salt mines, excavated nearly a thousand graves of the prehistoric cemetery and left records with watercolors of each one. Eduard von Sacken published the whole in 1868, and Hans Hildebrand took the site to name the early Iron Age. Excavations have continued to the present, run by the Natural History Museum in Vienna.

hechos/principados-hallstaticos/titulo.texto: The princely seats of the late Hallstatt period

hechos/principados-hallstaticos/resumen.texto: Between the last quarter of the 7th century BC and the middle of the 5th century BC, in southern Germany, eastern France and Switzerland, fortified hilltops arose (Heuneburg, Mont Lassois, Hohenasperg, Üetliberg), surrounded by mounds with very rich graves and Greek and Etruscan imports: wine, Attic pottery and bronzes. Wolfgang Kimmig called them “princely seats” (Fürstensitze). The term implies hereditary chiefs who controlled trade with the Mediterranean, an interpretation other archaeologists dispute because we do not know how that power was organized. Fernández-Götz and Krausse (2013) present them as the first cities north of the Alps.

hechos/muralla-de-adobe-de-la-heuneburg/.texto: The mudbrick rampart of the Heuneburg

Around 600 BC, the citadel of the Heuneburg was surrounded by a wall of mudbricks on a stone plinth, with rectangular towers. It was a Mediterranean technique without parallel north of the Alps, perhaps designed by someone who had seen Greek cities. Recent excavations also revealed an outer settlement of some 100 hectares. The wall was destroyed by fire and replaced by a rampart of local type.

hechos/tumba-de-hochdorf/resumen.texto: An adult man over 1.80 m tall was buried around 530 BC on a bronze couch almost three meters long, supported by female figures on wheels. With him were a torc, armlets and gold ornaments, a four-wheeled wagon, drinking horns, and a Greek cauldron with lions that had held mead. An amateur detected the grave in 1968, and Jörg Biel excavated it in 1978–1979. It is the only princely grave of the period that survived intact.

hechos/tumba-de-vix/resumen.texto: A woman was buried around 500-470 BC at the foot of Mont Lassois, on a wagon body, with a gold torc of nearly half a kilogram and the largest metal vessel known from classical antiquity: a Greek bronze krater 1.63 m tall, holding some 1,100 liters. René Joffroy and Maurice Moisson discovered it intact in 1953. That a woman had the richest grave in the region led to debate over whether she was a ruler or a priestess. Both readings are conjectures.

hechos/guerrero-de-hirschlanden/resumen.texto: Sandstone statue of a naked man wearing a conical helmet, a belt, a dagger and a torc, which crowned a mound of the Hallstatt culture. It was found in 1962. It is the oldest life-size human statue of the Iron Age north of the Alps, and its legs imitate Greek or Etruscan models.

hechos/guerrero-del-glauberg/resumen.texto: In 1996, next to the main mound of the Glauberg, a 1.86 m sandstone statue appeared of an early La Tène warrior with a shield, a sword, a torc and a headdress with two large leaves, similar to those worn by the figures in La Tène art. The neighboring grave had a bronze drinking jug and weapons. It is debated whether the statue represents the dead man, an ancestor or a god.

hechos/tartessos/resumen.texto: The Greeks called Tartessos a region rich in silver in the lower Guadalquivir and Huelva, in contact with the Phoenicians of Gadir from the 9th century BC. Herodotus tells of the arrival of Colaeus of Samos and the reign of Argantonius. Archaeology shows a mixed culture, local and Phoenician, with sanctuaries such as El Carambolo and Cancho Roano. Its language, that of the southwestern stelae, is not deciphered. John T. Koch reads it as Celtic, and most Paleohispanic specialists reject this.

hechos/fundacion-de-masalia/resumen.texto: Around 600 BC, colonists from Phocaea in Asia Minor founded Massalia near the mouth of the Rhône. According to Justin (XLIII.3), the Phocaean leader Protis married Gyptis, daughter of Nann, king of the Segobriges, who chose him as her husband at a banquet. Aristotle, cited by Athenaeus (XIII.576), tells the same story with other names. It is a foundation story that cannot be verified. From Massalia, wine, Greek pottery and bronzes reached the Rhône and the Saône as far as Mont Lassois and the Heuneburg.

hechos/fundacion-de-emporion/resumen.texto: Phocaeans from Massalia founded a trading port around 575 BC on an islet off the coast of Girona, and later on the mainland, next to the Iberian Indiketes. Strabo (III.4.8) and Livy (XXXIV.9) describe it as a double city, with walls separating Greeks and natives. It was the main gateway for Greek products into the Iberian Peninsula.

hechos/batalla-de-alalia/resumen.texto: Off Corsica, the Phocaeans who had settled at Alalia defeated, with heavy losses, an allied fleet of Etruscans and Carthaginians, according to Herodotus (I.166). Even as victors, they abandoned Corsica. The usual reading is that the division that followed left the south of the Iberian Peninsula under Carthaginian influence and halted Greek expansion in the western Mediterranean, although Greek trade with the peninsula continued.

hechos/cultura-de-villanova/resumen.texto: Early Iron Age culture of Etruria and Bologna, with biconical urns and cremation cemeteries, considered the initial phase of Etruscan civilization. Ancient DNA (Posth and others, 2021) shows that the Etruscans had the same ancestry as their Italic neighbors, including steppe ancestry, although they spoke a non-Indo-European language. Herodotus's thesis of a Lydian origin finds no genetic support.

hechos/cultura-de-golasecca/resumen.texto: Iron Age culture between Lakes Maggiore and Como and the Ticino river, in northern Italy and southern Switzerland, which controlled the Alpine passes between Etruria and the Hallstatt world. Many researchers link it to the Canegrate culture of the 13th century BC and regard it as that of the first Celtic speakers of Italy. Its Lepontic inscriptions are the oldest texts in a Celtic language. It declined after the Gaulish invasions of the 4th century BC.

hechos/primeras-inscripciones-celtas/tit.texto: The first inscriptions in a Celtic language

hechos/primeras-inscripciones-celtas/res.texto: In the Golasecca area, Lepontic speakers adapted the Etruscan alphabet (the “Lugano alphabet”) to write their language. According to the Lexicon Leponticum, the Castelletto Ticino vessel with the word “χosioiso” (“of Xosios”) dates to the second quarter of the 6th century BC, and the Prestino slab, with a dedication of several words, to the second quarter of the 5th. They are centuries earlier than any text in Gaulish, Celtiberian or Irish (unless the southwestern Iberian stelae are Celtic, as Koch argues and most scholars reject), and they prove there was Celtic in northern Italy before the Gaulish invasions.

hechos/cultura-de-la-tene/resumen.texto: Second Iron Age of central and western Europe, from the mid-5th century BC (La Tène A, around 450-380 BC) until the Roman conquest. It is marked by an art of its own of curves, palmettes and faces, two-wheeled war chariots, long swords and, from the 2nd century BC, large fortified settlements (oppida) and coins. Its objects reach from Ireland to Anatolia, which coincides with the migrations of Gauls into Italy and the Balkans recounted by Polybius and Livy. Since the late 19th century, and above all since Déchelette, it has been identified with the Celts. “Celtic skeptics” warn that material culture does not equal a people or a language, and in France the DNA (Fischer and others, 2022) does not show the arrival of a new population with it.

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-tene/titulo.texto: Discovery of the La Tène site

hechos/descubrimiento-de-la-tene/resumen.texto: In 1857, Hansli Kopp, who was looking for antiquities for Colonel Friedrich Schwab, pulled several iron weapons out of Lake Neuchâtel. The correction of the Jura waters lowered the lake level from 1868 and exposed remains of wooden bridges and thousands of objects, which Paul Vouga excavated systematically between 1907 and 1917. In 1872 Hildebrand took the site to name the second Iron Age.

hechos/jarras-de-basse-yutz/resumen.texto: A pair of bronze flagons inlaid with coral and red enamel, found in 1927 in Lorraine and now in the British Museum. They copy the shape of Etruscan jugs, but with handles in the form of animals and decoration in the early La Tène style. On the spout, a duck seems to swim toward the mouth. They show how Celtic art adapted Mediterranean models to the service of wine.

hechos/tumba-de-waldalgesheim/resumen.texto: Grave of a woman with a wagon, found in 1869 near Bingen, with a gold torc and armlets and a bronze bucket from southern Italy. Jacobsthal took its continuous tendril-scroll decoration to name the Waldalgesheim style, the second phase of La Tène art, which spread from Champagne to Italy and the Balkans.

hechos/casco-de-agris/resumen.texto: Ceremonial iron helmet covered with bronze, gold and coral, found in 1981 in a cave in Charente, in western France. Its decoration of palmettes and tendrils mixes the Waldalgesheim style with Greek and Etruscan motifs. It is one of the masterpieces of La Tène art.

hechos/lenguas-preindoeuropeas-de-europa.texto: Before the Indo-European languages, other languages were spoken in Europe, of which only traces survive: Basque and its ancestor Aquitanian, Iberian (readable but not understood), Etruscan and Raetic (related according to Rix), and words and place names with no Indo-European etymology in Celtic, Germanic and Greek. Whether Pictish was Celtic or non-Indo-European was debated until Katherine Forsyth (1997) argued that it was Brittonic. Hans Krahe attributed the oldest river names to an Indo-European “Old European,” and Theo Vennemann to a “Vasconic” family, theses that most linguists reject. Ancient DNA shows that the Basques have steppe ancestry like their neighbors, so keeping a language did not depend on avoiding migrations.

hechos/desciframiento-de-la-escritura-ib.texto: Manuel Gómez-Moreno showed that the Iberian script of the northeast and the Levante combined alphabetic signs for vowels and some consonants with syllabic signs for stops (a “semisyllabary”). He relied on the coin legends and on texts such as the Alcoy lead sheet, written in Greek letters. Since then Iberian texts can be read aloud, but the language remains untranslated. The old thesis that Iberian is ancient Basque (the “Basque-Iberian” hypothesis) has not been confirmed, although there are coincidences in sounds, names and perhaps numerals.

hechos/origen-de-las-lenguas-celtas/titu.texto: The origin of the Celtic languages

hechos/origen-de-las-lenguas-celtas/resu.texto: Proto-Celtic, reconstructed by comparing Gaulish, Celtiberian, Lepontic and the insular languages, must have formed before the 6th century BC, the date of the first inscriptions. In the 20th century it was placed in central Europe with Hallstatt and La Tène (“Celtic from the East,” Déchelette and Hubert). Renfrew (1987) had it arise in the west with the Neolithic farmers, Koch and Cunliffe (2010) on the Atlantic façade of the Bronze Age (“Celtic from the West”), and Sims-Williams (2020) in France in the first millennium BC. Patterson's DNA (2022) shows a migration from France to Britain around 1000-875 BC, and the studies of Brunel (2020) and Fischer (2022) show continuity between the Bronze and Iron Ages in France. None of those data says what language those people spoke.

hechos/cultura-chasense/resumen.texto: Middle Neolithic archaeological culture of France, in its periodization, dating from about 4500 to 3500 BC and named after the site of Chassey-le-Camp (Saône-et-Loire). It extended across the south (Occitania, Provence) and the northern plains and plateaus, in the Seine basin and the upper Loire. They were sedentary farmers and herders of sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, living in villages of 100 to 400 people, with sparsely decorated pottery, flint working and no metal; at Bercy (Paris, around 4000–3800 BC) wooden canoes have been found. Around 3500 BC it gave way to the Seine-Oise-Marne culture in the north and to other cultures in the south.

lugares/carnac/resumen.texto: More than three thousand stones raised in rows on the south coast of Brittany, along with dolmens and mounds, erected between the 5th and 4th millennia BC by Neolithic farmers, some three thousand years before Celtic was spoken in the region. Local tradition explained them as Roman soldiers turned to stone. Their function remains unknown.

lugares/barnenez/resumen.texto: A large stone cairn with eleven passage chambers on the north coast of Brittany, built in two stages from the middle of the 5th millennium BC. It is among the oldest megalithic monuments in Europe, which supports the idea that megalithism began in northwestern France.

lugares/dolmen-de-menga/resumen.texto: A large megalithic tomb at Antequera (Málaga), with slabs of more than a hundred tons and a pit at the bottom of the chamber, built around the 4th millennium BC. Its axis does not point to the sunrise but to the Peña de los Enamorados. It is a World Heritage Site together with the other dolmens of Antequera.

lugares/newgrange/resumen.texto: A large passage tomb in the Boyne valley, Ireland, built around 3200 BC, older than Stonehenge and the pyramids of Giza. At the winter solstice sunrise, light enters through an opening above the doorway and reaches the back of the chamber. Medieval Irish mythology made it the dwelling of the Túatha Dé Danann, but its builders lived some two thousand years before any trace of Celtic languages in Ireland.

lugares/skara-brae/resumen.texto: A Neolithic village in Orkney, with stone houses that preserve their beds, shelves and hearths, inhabited between the late 4th and mid-3rd millennia BC. A storm uncovered it in 1850.

lugares/stonehenge/resumen.texto: A stone monument on Salisbury Plain, built and reworked in several stages between 3000 and 1500 BC by Neolithic and Bronze Age populations. It is neither Celtic nor druidic: that attribution comes from the antiquaries of the 17th and 18th centuries (John Aubrey, William Stukeley). The bluestones come from Wales and the Altar Stone from northeastern Scotland.

lugares/avebury/resumen.texto: The largest stone circle in Britain, within a ditch and bank, raised in the 3rd millennium BC some 30 km from Stonehenge, with avenues of stones and nearby monuments such as Silbury Hill.

lugares/los-millares/resumen.texto: A walled Copper Age settlement in Almería, with several lines of walls, forts and a necropolis of collective tombs. It is one of the earliest copper metallurgy centers in western Europe.

lugares/hallstatt/resumen.texto: A village in the Austrian Alps beside salt mines worked since the Bronze Age. Its prehistoric cemetery, excavated since 1846, gave its name to the Hallstatt culture of the early Iron Age. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1997.

lugares/heuneburg/resumen.texto: A fortified hilltop above the Danube in southwestern Germany, a center of power of the Hallstatt culture in the 6th century BC, with a Mediterranean-style mudbrick wall and an outer settlement of some 100 hectares. It has been identified with Pyrene, the city of the Celts near the sources of the Danube that Herodotus mentions (II.33). The identification is possible but not proven.

lugares/magdalenenberg/resumen.texto: A Hallstatt-period mound near Villingen-Schwenningen, the largest in central Europe (about 33,000 m³), raised over a central wooden grave dated by dendrochronology to 616 BC. Looted already in antiquity, it contains more than a hundred secondary graves. Konrad Spindler excavated it between 1970 and 1973.

lugares/hochdorf/resumen.texto: A Hallstatt culture mound at Eberdingen (Baden-Württemberg), whose intact chamber held a man buried around 530 BC with gold grave goods, a bronze couch and a Greek cauldron. Today there is a museum there and a reconstruction of the mound.

lugares/vix-mont-lassois/resumen.texto: A fortified hilltop above the upper Seine in Burgundy, the center of the late Hallstatt culture, with a large apsidal building. It controlled the passage between the Seine and the Saône. At its foot lies the Vix grave.

lugares/glauberg/resumen.texto: A fortified hilltop in Hesse with mounds of the 5th and 4th centuries BC, a processional way and a large ditch. In 1996 a life-size stone statue of an early La Tène warrior appeared there.

lugares/golasecca/resumen.texto: A village in the province of Varese, beside the Ticino, where in the early 19th century the abbot Giovanni Battista Giani excavated some fifty graves that gave their name to the Golasecca culture, that of the Lepontic speakers.

lugares/la-tene/resumen.texto: A site on the shore of Lake Neuchâtel, in Switzerland, where from 1857 hundreds of swords, spears, shields, brooches and human remains emerged, along with the remains of wooden bridges. It gave its name to the La Tène culture of the second Iron Age. It is debated whether it was a place of offerings, a bridge or a battlefield.

lugares/masalia/resumen.texto: A Greek colony founded around 600 BC by Phocaeans from Asia Minor near the mouth of the Rhône, in the territory of the Ligurian Segobriges. It was the gateway for wine, pottery and Greek objects into Gaul and central Europe, and from there Pytheas set out for the North Atlantic.

lugares/emporion/resumen.texto: A Greek colony founded by Phocaeans from Massalia around 575 BC on the Girona coast, next to the Iberian Indiketes. Strabo (III.4.8) describes it as a double city, Greek and native. Rome landed there in 218 BC.

lugares/ullastret/resumen.texto: The largest Iberian settlement in Catalonia, probably the capital of the Indiketes, a few kilometers from Emporion, with walls, towers and neighborhoods from the 6th century BC until its abandonment around 200 BC. Its finds include Iberian inscriptions on lead and nailed severed heads, evidence of practices that classical authors also attributed to the Celts.

lugares/cancho-roano/resumen.texto: A palace building and sanctuary on the Tartessian periphery at Zalamea de la Serena (Badajoz), surrounded by a moat. It was rebuilt several times, and was burned and deliberately buried around the end of the 5th century BC. It shows the mix of local and Phoenician traditions of the southwestern peninsula.
